lesson.title: From Guesswork to Law: What Probability Really Means
lesson.summary: Probability puts a precise number on chance by describing the long run pattern that a random phenomenon settles into, even though no single outcome is predictable on its own.
lesson.body:
Probability is the branch of mathematics that puts a number on chance. A random phenomenon, like a coin flip or which household ends up in a sample, is unpredictable on any single trial, but its behavior settles into a stable, predictable pattern over many repetitions. Probability is the tool for describing that long run pattern precisely, and it is the mathematical foundation underneath nearly every statistical method used to draw conclusions from data, including the sampling ideas from earlier chapters. When a simple random sample gives every household a known chance of selection, that chance is a probability, and everything statisticians can later say about how trustworthy the resulting estimate is depends on that number being defined rigorously.

There are two related ways to arrive at a probability. Theoretical probability comes from a model of the situation, such as assuming a coin is fair or a die is balanced, and then counting outcomes: if a die has six equally likely faces, the theoretical probability of rolling any particular face is one sixth. Empirical, or experimental, probability instead comes from actually observing outcomes and calculating the relative frequency with which something happened, such as rolling a die 600 times and counting how many times a 4 appeared. The law of large numbers connects the two: as the number of trials grows very large, the empirical relative frequency gets closer and closer to the true theoretical probability. This is why casinos, insurance companies, and pollsters can rely on probability at scale even though no individual coin flip, claim, or survey respondent is predictable on its own.

The law of large numbers is also the source of one of the most persistent errors in probabilistic thinking, the gambler's fallacy, the belief that a fair coin is due for tails after a long run of heads. Independent trials have no memory. The coin does not know how many times it has landed heads, and the true probability of tails on the very next flip remains exactly one half no matter what came before. The law of large numbers describes what happens over thousands of flips, not what a single flip owes to correct an earlier imbalance.

Probability calculations often rest on identifying outcomes that cannot happen at the same time and adding their individual probabilities together, an idea called the addition rule that later chapters will develop fully. As a first example, consider rolling one fair six sided die and asking for the probability of rolling an even number. The outcomes 2, 4, and 6 cannot occur simultaneously on a single roll, so their probabilities can simply be added: P(even) = P(2) + P(4) + P(6), which is one sixth plus one sixth plus one sixth, equaling three sixths, or one half. This matches intuition directly, since exactly three of the six equally likely faces are even.

Probability matters to statistics for a very practical reason: it lets researchers quantify how surprising a particular sample result would be if some underlying claim about the population were actually true. That quantified surprise is the seed of statistical inference, the subject that everything in this course eventually builds toward. Before any of that is possible, though, probability needs a small set of formal rules that guarantee the arithmetic always behaves sensibly, which is exactly where the next chapter begins.
